lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Types of Feed for Different Animals

pages.body:
A goat tied behind a house chews grass and cassava peels all day. In a poultry house nearby, hens peck at a fine mixture poured from a printed bag. A pig in its pen eats kitchen leftovers and a mash of maize bran.

- Why are these animals not all given the same food?
- What do you think is inside the bag of poultry feed?

Feed is any material given to farm animals to supply the nutrients they need. In Basic 7 you grouped farm animals into ruminants, monogastrics and poultry. In this lesson we group feeds into types, match each type to the animals that can use it and learn what nutrients each feed supplies.

We begin with the main groups of feed.

pages.title: Types of animal feed
pages.body:
| **Type of feed** | **Description** | **Examples** |
|---|---|---|
| Roughages | Bulky feeds that are high in fibre and low in nutrients for their size. They may be fresh or dry | Grasses such as elephant grass and guinea grass, legumes such as centrosema, hay, silage, straw and maize stalks |
| Concentrates | Feeds that are low in fibre and rich in energy or protein | Energy concentrates such as maize, sorghum, wheat bran and cassava chips. Protein concentrates such as fish meal, soya bean meal and groundnut cake |
| Supplements | Feeds given in small amounts to supply minerals or vitamins | Oyster shell, bone meal, salt lick and vitamin premix |
| Additives | Substances added in very small amounts to improve health or growth | Medicines that prevent disease in chicks, and enzymes that help digestion |

Fresh green grass and legumes are called forage or pasture. Hay is grass that has been cut and dried. Silage is green fodder that has been chopped, packed without air and allowed to ferment so that it keeps for the dry season. A compound or formulated feed is a mixture of several ingredients in fixed proportions, such as layer mash.

Next we match the types of feed to the animals that can use them.

questions.e: Silage is green fodder that has been chopped, packed without air and allowed to ferment so that it keeps for the dry season.

pages.title: Matching feed to animals
pages.body:
| **Group of animals** | **Examples** | **Main feed** | **Reason** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ruminants | Cattle, sheep, goats | Mostly roughages, with some concentrates and a salt lick | Microorganisms in the rumen break down fibre, so ruminants can live on grass |
| Monogastric animals | Pigs, rabbits | Pigs are fed concentrates, kitchen waste and tubers. Rabbits are fed green leaves with some concentrate | A simple stomach cannot digest much fibre, although the rabbit digests some in its large caecum |
| Poultry | Chickens, ducks, turkeys, guinea fowl | Concentrates in the form of mash, crumbs or pellets, with grit and oyster shell | Birds have no teeth and a short gut, so they need fine, rich feed that is quickly digested |
| Fish | Tilapia, catfish | Floating or sinking pellets rich in protein | Fish grow fast and need a high level of protein |
Now we look at the nutrients that feed must supply and where each comes from.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Nutrients in feed and their sources

pages.title: Nutrients in feed and their sources
pages.body:
| **Nutrient** | **Use in the body of the animal** | **Sources in feed** |
|---|---|---|
| Carbohydrates | Supply energy for movement, body heat and production | Maize, sorghum, millet, cassava, wheat bran, rice bran |
| Proteins | Build muscle, repair tissues and form milk, eggs and young ones | Fish meal, soya bean meal, groundnut cake, cotton seed cake, blood meal, legumes |
| Fats and oils | Supply concentrated energy and help the body to use some vitamins | Palm kernel cake, groundnut cake, soya bean, palm oil |
| Minerals | Calcium and phosphorus build bones, teeth and eggshells. Iron forms blood. Salt keeps body fluids in balance | Oyster shell, bone meal, limestone, salt lick |
| Vitamins | Protect the animal from disease and keep the body working well | Green leaves, yellow maize, vitamin premix, sunlight for vitamin D |
| Water | Needed for every process in the body | Clean drinking water and fresh green feed |

A ration is the amount of feed given to an animal in one day. A balanced ration contains all the nutrients in the right amounts and proportions for the kind, age and purpose of the animal.

> **Did you know?** Hens are given crushed oyster shell because each eggshell needs about two grams of calcium, which is more than ordinary feed can supply.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Selecting Feed from the Label on the Bag

pages.body:
A new poultry farmer goes to a feed shop and sees bags marked chick starter, grower mash, layer mash, broiler starter and broiler finisher. All the bags look alike, yet the prices and the small print on the labels differ.

- How can the farmer know which bag to buy for day old chicks?
- What information do you expect to find printed on a feed bag?

Manufactured feeds are sold in bags with a label that states what the feed contains. In this lesson we learn to read a feed label and to choose the right feed for an animal from the proportions of nutrients shown.

We start with the information printed on a feed bag.

questions.q: Day old broiler chicks should be fed on
questions.e: A new poultry farmer goes to a feed shop and sees bags marked chick starter, grower mash, layer mash, broiler starter and broiler finisher.

pages.title: What a feed label shows
pages.body:
- The name of the feed and the animal and age it is meant for.
- The proportion of each nutrient, written as a percentage. This is sometimes called the guaranteed analysis.
- The list of ingredients.
- The net weight of the bag, for example 50 kg.
- Directions for feeding and storage.
- The name of the manufacturer, the batch number, the date of manufacture and the expiry date.

| **Term on the label** | **Meaning** |
|---|---|
| Crude protein | The proportion of protein in the feed. It is the most important figure for growth and for egg and milk production |
| Crude fibre | The proportion of tough plant material. Poultry and pig feeds must be low in fibre |
| Crude fat | The proportion of fats and oils, which supply concentrated energy |
| Calcium and phosphorus | Minerals for bones and eggshells. Feed for laying birds is high in calcium |
| Metabolisable energy | The amount of energy the animal can actually use from each kilogram of feed |
| Moisture | The proportion of water. Feed with too much moisture grows mould in storage |
Next we compare typical labels for different kinds and ages of chicken.

o: Amount of water in the feed
Proportion of protein in the feed
questions.e: In this lesson we learn to read a feed label and to choose the right feed for an animal from the proportions of nutrients shown.

pages.title: Comparing feeds for poultry
pages.body:
| **Feed** | **Given to** | **Crude protein** | **Calcium** | **Why** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Chick starter | Chicks from day old to about 8 weeks | About 20 percent | About 1 percent | Young birds grow very fast and need much protein |
| Grower mash | Pullets from about 9 to 18 weeks | About 15 to 16 percent | About 1 percent | Growth is slower and the birds must not become too fat before laying |
| Layer mash | Hens that are laying | About 16 to 18 percent | About 3.5 to 4 percent | High calcium is needed for strong eggshells and protein for the egg itself |
| Broiler starter | Meat birds in the first 3 to 4 weeks | About 22 to 23 percent | About 1 percent | Very fast growth of muscle needs the highest protein |
| Broiler finisher | Meat birds from about 4 weeks to market | About 18 to 20 percent | About 1 percent | More energy and a little less protein to add weight before sale |

The figures are typical values. The exact figures differ a little from one manufacturer to another, so the label on the bag must always be read.

Now we set out the steps for choosing the right bag.

questions.q: Which feed has the highest proportion of calcium?
questions.e: A compound or formulated feed is a mixture of several ingredients in fixed proportions, such as layer mash.

pages.title: Rules for choosing a feed
pages.body:
1. Identify the kind of animal, its age and its purpose, such as growth, eggs, meat, milk or breeding.
2. Read the name on the bag and check that it is made for that animal and that age.
3. Check the crude protein. Young, fast growing and producing animals need more protein than mature animals that are only being maintained.
4. Check the calcium. Laying birds need a feed with a high level of calcium.
5. Check the crude fibre. Choose low fibre feed for poultry and pigs.
6. Check the expiry date and the condition of the bag. Do not buy feed that is damp, lumpy, mouldy or has a bad smell.

Giving the wrong feed wastes money and harms the animals. Chicks fed on layer mash receive too much calcium, which can damage their kidneys, and too little protein for good growth. Laying hens fed on grower mash lay eggs with thin shells because the feed has too little calcium.

Finally we see how to keep feed in good condition.

pages.title: Storing feed
pages.body:
- Store bags in a cool, dry, airy room on wooden pallets, away from the floor and the walls.
- Keep out rats, birds and insects.
- Use the oldest bags first.
- Never give mouldy feed to animals. Moulds produce poisons that can kill poultry.

> **Did you know?** Feed is the largest cost in poultry and pig farming. It usually takes more than half of all the money the farmer spends.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: The Importance of Water and Feed to Animals

pages.body:
During a long dry season a farmer forgets to fill the water trough in the goat pen for two days. The goats stop eating, stand with their heads down and their eyes look sunken. The nanny goats give very little milk.

- Why did the goats stop eating when they had no water?
- What do you think will happen if they get no water for several more days?

An animal can live for weeks with little feed but only a few days without water. In this lesson we explain why water and feed are needed for growth and reproduction, and we predict what happens to animals that do not get enough water.

We begin with the uses of water in the body of an animal.

questions.q: Which animals can live mainly on grass?
questions.e: The goats stop eating, stand with their heads down and their eyes look sunken.

pages.title: The importance of water
pages.body:
- Water makes up more than half of the body mass of an animal. Blood, milk and eggs are mostly water. Milk is about 87 percent water and an egg is about three quarters water.
- Water softens feed and is needed for digestion.
- Water carries digested food, oxygen and hormones around the body in the blood.
- Water removes waste from the body in urine and droppings.
- Water cools the body through sweating and panting.
- Water is needed for the production of milk, eggs and semen, and for the growth of the young inside the mother.
- Water keeps joints moving smoothly and cushions organs.

The amount of water an animal needs depends on its size, the weather, the type of feed and what it is producing. Animals that eat dry feed, animals in hot weather and animals that are giving milk or laying eggs drink the most. As a guide, a laying hen drinks about a quarter of a litre a day and a mature cow drinks tens of litres a day. Clean, cool water should be available at all times.

Next we look at what feed does for growth and reproduction.

questions.q: Which of the following is a use of water in the body of an animal?
questions.e: Body temperature rises because the animal cannot cool itself.

pages.title: The importance of feed
pages.body:
| **Use of feed** | **Explanation** |
|---|---|
| Maintenance | Supplies energy to keep the animal alive, warm and active even when it is not growing or producing |
| Growth | Protein, minerals and energy build new muscle, bone and other tissues in young animals |
| Reproduction | Well fed animals come on heat at the right time, produce healthy eggs and sperm, carry the young to full term and give birth to strong offspring |
| Production | Extra nutrients are turned into milk, eggs, meat and wool |
| Health | Vitamins and minerals help the animal to resist disease and to recover quickly from illness |
| Work | Draught animals such as bullocks and donkeys need energy for ploughing and carrying loads |

Animals that are underfed grow slowly, become thin and weak, fall sick easily, mature late and may fail to breed. Mothers that are underfed give birth to small, weak young and produce little milk. Animals that are overfed become too fat, which also lowers fertility and wastes feed.

Finally we predict the effects of a shortage of water.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: What happens to animals without adequate water

pages.title: What happens to animals without adequate water
pages.body:
1. The animal eats less, because dry feed cannot be swallowed and digested without water.
2. Milk yield and egg laying fall sharply. Hens may stop laying within a day or two.
3. The animal loses body mass and growth stops.
4. The animal becomes dehydrated. The signs are sunken eyes, a dry nose and mouth, dry skin that stays folded when pinched, dark and scanty urine, and hard, dry droppings.
5. Body temperature rises because the animal cannot cool itself. This is called heat stress.
6. Waste products build up in the blood and damage the kidneys.
7. Pregnant animals may lose their young, and breeding is delayed.
8. If the shortage continues, the animal collapses and dies.

Dirty water is also harmful. It spreads diseases and parasites, so drinkers and troughs should be washed every day.

[[pic: Two drawings of a goat side by side. The first shows a healthy goat with a bright coat, clear eyes and a full water trough. The second shows a dehydrated goat with sunken eyes, a dull coat, a drooping head and an empty trough.]]

> **Did you know?** A chicken has no sweat glands. It cools itself by panting and by drinking, which is why poultry die quickly when water runs out on a hot day.

questions.e: The signs are sunken eyes, a dry nose and mouth, dry skin that stays folded when pinched, dark and scanty urine, and hard, dry droppings.

pages.body:
- Feed is any material given to farm animals to supply nutrients. The main types are roughages, concentrates, supplements and additives.
- Ruminants are fed mostly roughages because microorganisms in the rumen digest fibre. Pigs and poultry need concentrates that are low in fibre.
- Feed supplies carbohydrates and fats for energy, proteins for growth and production, minerals for bones and eggshells, vitamins for health, and water.
- A balanced ration contains all the nutrients in the right amounts for the kind, age and purpose of the animal.
- A feed label shows the name of the feed, the proportions of nutrients such as crude protein, crude fibre and calcium, the ingredients, the weight and the expiry date.
- Young and fast growing animals need feed with more protein. Laying birds need feed with more calcium.
- Water is needed for digestion, transport, removal of waste, cooling, and the production of milk and eggs.
- Animals without adequate water eat less, produce less, lose mass, become dehydrated and finally die.
